chapter.title: Two Clocks
chapter.sub: The long takes click. The short ones never do. Everyone has a theory; the fault has a watch.

items.text: SEASON 10 · EPISODE 1 · DRAFT · CASE-050  Coldframe Sound, Studio A · week one of six · Maya, Hollis (owner and chief engineer), Pim (assistant engineer) and Esme (the artist) · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  Maya takes a six-week contract on one small room, on purpose. The album is due at the label in six weeks. The long takes click, the short ones don’t, and everyone has a theory.  ⚑ RV-176: the performance is Esme’s; the studio is Hollis’s. RV-177: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on the loadout your Season 9 review locked.

items.title: Two Clocks
items.stakes: The long takes click and the short ones don't. The album is due in six weeks, and Esme sings the ballad at two.
items.reward: A clean ten-minute take — and a studio with one leader.

objectives.text: Decide what stops the next one

items.rumor: A fault that keeps time is telling you something.

items.sub: Monday · 10:40 a.m. · Studio A control room

items.alt: Studio A's control room at Coldframe Sound: fabric panels, a window into the live room, two monitors on stands and a long console; Hollis, grey-bearded in a cardigan, points at the speakers; Maya listens.

bubbles.text: There. One minute seven in. Every long take, one click. Short takes, never.
Play me the next one. Don't touch anything.

items.caption: Six weeks to the album.

lines.text: It's the ghost. Came free with the building in ninety-six.
Then your ghost has a very good watch.

items.prompt: 11:00. Long takes click; short ones never do. Esme arrives at two. What first?
items.risk: A ghost hunt that eats the day — or a fault hidden in the best takes.
timeout: Esme sings at two into the same fault.

hints.text: What would the fault look like if you gave it long enough to happen?

options.label: Recable the live room before two
options.result: Four hours of recabling. At 14:40 the ballad clicks again, in the same place.
options.consequence: A change before a measurement — and every cable you touched is now a new suspect.

options.label: Before touching anything, record ten minutes of tone on every input and mark each click: which channels, how far apart
options.result: A click every 66.7 seconds — only on the converter's sixteen channels. The stage boxes are clean.
options.consequence: Measure the fault on its own terms: longer than it takes to appear.

options.label: Raise the interface's input buffer so it absorbs the clicks
options.result: The clicks now come every four and a half minutes. Fewer takes click. Nobody knows why.
options.consequence: Hides the fault and keeps it.

options.label: Ask Esme to sing the ballad in sections under a minute
options.result: Esme: “It's a four-minute song. I don't sing it in pieces.”
options.consequence: Changing the performance to dodge a fault isn't yours to ask.

items.title: Sixty-seven seconds.
items.body: Maya lays the ten-minute test against a timeline. The clicks don't wander: 66.7 s, 133.3 s, 200 s — like a metronome set far too slow. Only the converter's sixteen channels click; the stage boxes on the network never do. Ghosts don't keep time. Clocks do.
items.label: Test: what clock difference makes exactly this interval?

items.sub: Mastery · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Pim and Maya beside a board. Hollis says the room's haunted. I say it's a cable. It only clicks on the long takes. Sixty-seven seconds apart, every time. Ghosts don't keep time. So what does? …Something counting?

bubbles.text: Hollis says the room's haunted. I say it's a cable. It only clicks on the long takes.
Sixty-seven seconds apart, every time. Ghosts don't keep time. So what does?

items.caption: Mastery: nobody hands you the tool. Pick it, and say why.

items.label: **Learn it now:** clocks — one leader, everyone follows.

items.text: 📖 From the Fieldbook · tap a plate to open it full size     Point it at people, not at the ceiling     The studio camera — image settings and standards     The first step to networking, AV style

items.alt: A test sheet: ten minutes of tone on every input. The converter's channels, drawn as an amber waveform, carry red click marks at 66.7, 133.3 and 200 seconds and every 66.7 seconds after; the stage-box channels, in blue, are clean. Note: takes under a minute never click.
items.caption: The fault keeps better time than the band.

items.title: ballad · take 7 · ‘ghost again’
items.body: Pim's session notes from last month, in pencil: ‘Ballad take 7 — ghost again, 1:07 and 2:13.’ Nobody had subtracted the two times. Sixty-six seconds.

items.title: The watch that kept the time
items.body: In 1761 a clockmaker's marine watch sailed from Portsmouth to Jamaica to prove that a ship could carry its home port's time across an ocean — and so work out its longitude. After 81 days at sea it had lost only about five seconds. What mattered wasn't that it was a good clock. It was that the whole ship could agree to follow one.

items.text: Act II — “The warning that went away”

items.title: Two leaders.
items.body: Maya reads every clock source. The interface leads the network. The converter leads itself — set to internal clock. Pim goes quiet, then says it: in the spring, when the interface arrived, the converter kept showing a lock warning on external clock, so Pim set it to internal and the warning went away. Nobody had plugged the word-clock cable in. The warning was right for four months.
items.label: Test: why did the warning disappear — and where did the fault go?

items.alt: The control room, late afternoon. Pim, in a teal hoodie, stands with his hands at his sides; Maya faces him, calm.

bubbles.text: I just wanted the warning gone. It was red all the time.
It was red because it was right. Next time, bring it to someone.

items.prompt: Are you going to tell Hollis it was me?

options.label: “You'll tell him, and I'll be there. The warning was the most honest thing in the room — you just didn't have anyone to ask.”
options.reply: …Okay. Can I ask you things? Like, all the time?

options.label: “It doesn't matter who. It matters that the next warning gets written up.”
options.reply: Right. Written up. Not switched off.

items.risk: Clicks in every long take of the album.
timeout: Esme's ballad goes down with two clocks in the room.

hints.text: How many leaders should there be — and does it matter which?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S10E01). Mastery: two answers are defensible.

options.label: The interface stays the leader; the converter follows it over word clock; the network follows the interface as before
options.result: One cable plugged in, one setting changed. Every lock light green.
options.consequence: One leader — the simplest chain that's already half built.

options.label: The old word-clock generator leads; the interface follows it and still serves the network; the converter follows the generator
options.result: Two cables, two settings. Every lock light green — and one more box whose failure stops the studio.
options.consequence: Also one leader. Defensible: Hollis trusts the old box; it adds a dependency.

options.label: Every device on its own internal clock — ‘each one stable’
options.consequence: Stable clocks, disagreeing — the exact fault, everywhere.
options.fail: Every device on its own clock is the fault itself.

options.label: Leave both, and put a sample-rate converter on the converter's input
options.result: It works — with a converter in the path that alters the audio slightly and adds delay, and a second clock still in the room.
options.consequence: A patch over a design problem.

items.label: **Fix it:** one leader for Studio A.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #92 · AVERY'S LENS  One clock leads; everything else follows  Digital audio devices must agree on when each sample happens. Pick one leader, make every other device follow it — and treat a lock warning as evidence, not noise.  A converter set to its own clock ‘to make the warning go away’ put a click into every take longer than a minute — for four months.

items.alt: A clock map after the fix: the interface is the one leader; the stage boxes and cue mixers follow the network; the converter follows the interface over a word-clock cable; the old generator is marked spare, not in the chain. Note: the generator would also have been one leader — Hollis chose the interface.
items.caption: One leader. Everything else follows.

items.title: page 31 · ‘EXT UNLOCK’
items.body: The converter's manual, page 31: ‘EXT UNLOCK: the unit cannot lock to the external reference. Check the reference cable and the leader's output.’ The word-clock cable from the interface had never been plugged in. The warning was right.

items.prompt: What stops the next click — and the next silenced warning?
items.happening: One leader; the ballad is clean.
unknown: What the next device will do when it arrives
items.risk: The same fault the next time anything is plugged in.
timeout: The next device arrives into a studio with no map.

hints.text: Who would notice a device falling off the leader — and how fast?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S10E01). Option B needs Monitoring & tools at LIMITED or better.

options.label: A sticker on the converter: DO NOT CHANGE
options.result: The sticker lasts until the next piece of gear arrives.

options.label: Lock-status monitoring on every clocked device, alarming in the control room; a clock map on the wall; a ten-minute tone test in the session-start sheet; warnings written up, never silenced
options.result: Hollis funds the monitoring. Pim draws the map and writes the first entry in a new ‘warnings’ page.
options.consequence: Watched, drawn, tested — and a culture where a red light gets asked about.

options.label: Session-start sheet only: Pim checks every lock light and records a ten-minute tone test each morning
options.result: It works while Pim remembers. The morning he's ill, nobody does.
options.consequence: The best you can do without monitoring — and it depends on one person.

options.label: Replace the converter with a newer one
options.result: A new converter — which also needs to follow the leader.

items.alt: The control room in the evening; Esme, in an amber jumper with locs tied back, grins after the ballad; Maya beside the console.

bubbles.text: Four minutes and not one click. I sang it straight through.
It was never you. It was two clocks arguing.

items.alt: Outside Coldframe Sound at night: an old glasshouse with warm windows and a painted sign by the door. Hollis points at his car, its door open; Maya listens.

bubbles.text: Listen to that. Last week's mix. In the room it's lovely. Out here it shakes the mirrors.
How long has it done that?

items.caption: Next: *The Mix That Only Sounded Good Here.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A fault that keeps time is a clue: time it, on every input, for longer than it takes to appear. Digital audio needs one clock leader; every other device follows it. Two good clocks are still two clocks — a buffer only decides how long it takes to click. Treat a lock warning as evidence, not noise. Either leader can be right; two leaders never are.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Which warning in your world have people learned to switch off instead of ask about?
